verses.text: When Johannes Gutenberg started printing the Bible in Mainz in the 1540s, he hired illustrators who would illuminate the first letter of each chapter with a hand-painted initial, thus imitating the late-medieval illuminated manuscripts produced in the monasteries at the time. The 1560 Geneva Bible has adopted this art, though it already uses pre-casted sorts instead of hand-painted initials, as do later the 1582 Rheims New Testament or the very famous 1611 King James Bible. The Irish-American Catholic printing press has later adopted an even simpler technique under ongoing industrilization: the 1899 Baltimore edition of the Douay-Rheims Bible, now in reprint by Saint Benedict Press and Baronius Press, uses two-line drop caps set in what appears to be Bodoni or Didot instead of fully-fledged initials. The New York prints of the Douay-Rheims Bible at the time, such as an 1885 edition by Bryan Taylor & Co., an 1899 edition by the Benzinger Brothers, or a 1914 edition by P. J. Kenedy & Sons, share the same drop caps. The Benzinger Brothers got their printing plates from M. H. Gill & Son in Dublin. By the mid-20th century, we would see the art of the initial disappear almost completely from public bookshelves: the Jerusalem Bible editions by Éditions du Cerf, or in English by Doubleday & Company, Inc. and later Darton, Longman & Todd Ltd. come with only the chapter number as a drop cap at the beginning of each chapter, and the 1952 Revised Standard Version by Thomas Nelson & Sons comes with nothing that even slightly resembles an initial. In Germany also, it is difficult to find a Luther Bible with drop caps that is earlier than the mid-19th century, even though Dr. Martin Luther’s own 1545 edition came with printed initials.

“The King’s printer” Robert Barker, when he printed the 1611 King James Version of the Bible, faced the issue that he seemingly wanted a new line for every new verse. To separate paragraphs in the biblical text then, he used the pilcrow glyph (¶) instead of line breaks. When you see the pilcrow (¶) in the 1611 KJV, therefore, know that there begins a new paragraph, and thereby a new subject matter: such as, for example, here in Genesis 1 where each day begins with a pilcrow. (See Acts 20:36 for more.)

Seeing the word “Heaven”, I must make a confession. Saint Benedict Press and Baronius Press have since the turn of the century undergone the effort of distributing a Douay-Rheims Bible that is a near fascimile of the famous 1899 Baltimore edition of the Douay-Rheims Bible, published by John Murphy Company, “Printers to the Holy See,” and with an imprimatur by James Cardinal Gibbons, the Archbishop of Baltimore and head of the American Catholic Church at the time. However, I have not used a specimen of this edition to produce the digital text that is here named “1899 Baltimore Douay-Rheims Bible”, because I do not possess an original specimen, only two reprints by the aforementioned two publishers. Instead, I have digitally reconstructed the 1899 Baltimore text from two other editions. One of them is a scan of an 1899 reprint produced by the Benzinger Brothers, who purchased the printing plates for a Douay-Rheims Bible from Patrick Donahoe. Patrick Donahoe was an Irish-American publisher who used these plates to reprint an 1846 Belfast edition of the Douay-Rheims Bible, appropriated by a man named “the Most Rev. Dr. Denvir.” Bishop Cornelius Denvir, in turn, reprinted an edition he got in Dublin. The 1899 Benzinger Brothers edition credits M. H. Gill & Son on the title page, who were the printers for the University of Dublin. Hence, the 1899 Benzinger Brothers edition is a reprint of a reprint of reprint from Dublin. It was, however, published not in Dublin, but in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago, thus adding to the chaos that was the 19th-century Irish-American Catholic printing press. By the time the Benzinger Brothers purchased the printing plates, they had already deteriorated over many years of usage. Here in this verse, the letter H in “Heaven” is missing its lower half. Letters missing their legs and arms can be observed throughout the 1899 Benzinger Brothers edition. None of this is seen when reading the digital text of the 1899 Baltimore edition here, but be assured that a lot of research went into confirming the validity of each verse of the 1899 Baltimore Douay-Rheims Bible, which under Saint Benedict Press is instead so hastily printed and distributed.

In a 1899 Benzinger Brothers edition of the Douay-Rheims Bible as well as in a 1914 reprint by P. J. Kenedy & Sons, the word “fruit tree” in this verse has a hyphen (= “fruit-tree”). I cannot confirm with certainty if the 1899 Baltimore edition has this word with a hyphen or not, because I do not own an original specimen; but reprints by Saint Benedict Press and Baronius Press as well as online versions of the 1899 Baltimore text (such as those on Project Gutenberg or Bible Gateway) have it without. The Benzinger Brothers got their printing plates from M. H. Hill & Son in Dublin, so it is likely that the hyphenated form is the original European one. It seems John Murphy Company under James Cardinal Gibbons has, with the authority of the Holy See, americanized the text of the Douay-Rheims Bible in certain areas by removing hyphens which are commonly used in European English. I laid my eyes upon a handful of cases where the hyphen was removed for the 1899 Baltimore edition, but there may be well over a hundred in total. There are also other differences between the 1899 Baltimore edition and the 1899 Benzinger Brothers edition, such as European spellings that were changed to American spellings in the Baltimore edition. (See Daniel 1:4 for more.)
